lines.text: This 40 year old motor oil has graphite in it and the can promises better gas mileage so he tests it against modern oil.
Graphite is slippery pencil lead because its carbon sheets slide over each other like a deck of cards.
beats: ai:close up of a sharpened wooden pencil tip with shiny dark graphite lead on white paper
ai:microscopic layers of flat black graphite carbon sheets sliding across each other
ai:a deck of playing cards sliding apart smoothly on a wooden table

lines.text: He cooks both at 400 degrees and the Arco loses 30 grams while Quaker State loses just 14.
So the old oil evaporates twice as much and leaves sludge at the bottom.
But on the friction tester the Arco leaves a way smaller wear scar which he never expected.
Because the lab finds almost 3 times more zinc and phosphorus which are anti wear additives that coat the metal.
beats: ai:a thin glossy protective oil film coating a polished steel engine bearing macro

lines.text: But on a full tank the generator with Arco dies 20 seconds sooner.
So that gas mileage promise never shows up.
And graphite powder in a worn mower raises compression from 95 to 105 psi.
But he'd never use it in a modern car because it could harm the catalytic converter.
beats: ai:a car catalytic converter cut open showing its ceramic honeycomb core glowing hot

lines.text: So would you pour graphite in your engine?
